title: In the beginning, Being alone (6.2)
hook: the father goes back to the beginning: there was only Being, one, without a second
carry: it thought: let me be many

segments.voice: Yesterday: the clay. Know one lump, and you know every pot. Your line was know the clay.

But what was there before? Before Grandma, before the dinosaurs, before the world? Kids ask it at bedtime. Philosophers ask it for a living. The Upanishads ask it too. Uddalaka has told his son that under every pot there's clay. Now Shvetaketu needs to know what the clay of everything is. So the father goes back to the beginning, with a creation story short enough for bedtime.
screen: `BUT WHAT WAS THERE BEFORE?` → `IN THE BEGINNING.` → `THE CLAY OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka begins: sad eva somyedam agra asit, ekam evadvitiyam. In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second. Sat: Being, what is. Then he takes on a rival view head-on. Some say that in the beginning there was non-being, and Being came out of it. But how could something come from nothing? No, my dear. In the beginning there was Being. Then the turn that gives today's line. That Being thought: let me be many. Let me grow forth. It sends out heat. The heat, in turn, thinks: let me be many, and sends out water. That's why, Uddalaka says, when a person is hot or grieving, they sweat or weep: water comes out of heat. The water thinks the same thought, and sends out food. That's why, wherever it rains, there's plenty to eat. Heat, water, food: the three basic stuffs everything else will be made of. Fire, water, food: Uddalaka keeps building big ideas out of the kitchen. And notice the motive. The text names nothing outside Being that makes it act. It simply thinks, let me be many. Later Hindu thinkers read that line in more than one way. Some hear the one truly becoming the many. Others hear the one appearing as many while staying one. The text just tells the story, and leaves the rest for the lessons to come.
screen: `BEING ALONE, ONE WITHOUT A SECOND.` · `HOW COULD BEING COME FROM NOTHING?` · `IT THOUGHT: LET ME BE MANY.` · `HEAT, THEN WATER, THEN FOOD.` · then, large: `SAD EVA SOMYEDAM AGRA ASIT.`

segments.voice: Let the room fade, the sounds, the light, the chair, and let your thoughts thin out until there's little left but the plain fact of being here. Rest there, and when something arises on its own, a sound, a thought, a sensation, watch the one becoming many, and let it come and go.
Sat, Being, what is, the real. Uddalaka's creation story: Being alone, one without a second, which thought, let me be many, and became heat, water and food.
Your line: it thought: let me be many. Heat first, then water, then food. That's day three hundred forty-one.

howItsDone: Uddalaka's opening line, 'Being alone, one without a second', is quoted again and again in Hindu philosophy, and Vedanta teachers use ekam evadvitiyam as a short summary of their teaching.

original.note: Sanskrit sat: being, what is, the real. Uddalaka's word for what was there in the beginning.

trapdoor: what you thought: a creation myth, like many others.
what it means: one Being, needing nothing, thinks let me be many, and becomes heat, water and food, the stuff of everything.
what a scholar hears: Chandogya 6.2.1–4. sad eva somyedam agra asit, ekam evadvitiyam; it names and rejects the view that non-being came first, a view the Taittiriya Upanishad (2.7) states.

chat.says: Does that Upanishad say the world came out of nothing?
options: Uddalaka says Being alone came first. It thought, let me be many, and became heat, water, food.
Uddalaka says food came first, and heat and water slowly grew out of the food.
Uddalaka says Being didn't want to change, but heat from outside forced it to.
chat.meaning: Uddalaka rejects being from non-being: in the beginning was Being alone, which thought, let me be many, and became heat, water and food.
